title: Anti-Government Protests Resurge in North Africa
gist: Foreign Policy's Africa Brief reports that 122°F heat plus 14-hour daily power cuts triggered simultaneous anti-government protests in Tripoli and Tunis, with Libyan demonstrators briefly shutting central bank branches and the Mellitah Oil and Gas complex and 150-200 heat deaths reported in Tunisia since blackouts began July 12. The brief also flags Chad's U.S.-pressured ICC withdrawal, Senegal's Faye-Sonko rupture jeopardizing an IMF deal, and Chinese Belt and Road investment in Africa nearly tripling to a record $33.5 billion in H1 2026.

themes.theme: Heat-plus-blackout as a protest trigger in North Africa

insights.claim: Libya, despite being a petrostate, is running daily 14-hour power cuts driven by years of underinvestment in critical infrastructure, pushing hundreds of demonstrators to block major roads in Tripoli as temperatures hit 122 degrees Fahrenheit.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: Resource wealth is no buffer against grid failure; Libyan political risk is now driven by domestic electricity capacity, not just oil price.
insights.quote: Although a petrostate, Libya is experiencing an electricity crisis driven by years of underinvestment in critical infrastructure.
insights.locator: Although a petrostate, Libya is experiencing an electricity crisis

insights.claim: Libyan protesters shut down branches of the country's central bank and forced the Mellitah Oil and Gas complex west of Tripoli to briefly suspend operations, while blocking entrances to government buildings, state television, and the state telecom company with trucks of soil and rubble.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: Libyan protest now has a direct kill-switch on hydrocarbon export infrastructure—a supply-disruption channel to watch while oil is already stressed by the Iran war.
insights.locator: Libyan protesters shut down branches of the country’s central bank

insights.claim: Although the Libyan protests occurred only in western Libya, demonstrators demanded removal of both the eastern and western rival governments, chanting 'Electricity—where have the billions gone?'
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: Anger is aimed at the whole divided political settlement rather than one faction, which removes the usual pressure valve of blaming the rival government.
insights.locator: The protests only took place in western Libya

insights.claim: Between 150 and 200 people have died in Tunisia since power cuts began on July 12, 2026, according to the Organisation of Young Doctors in Tunisia, with extreme heat also triggering at least 900 wildfires across the country in a single three-day period.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
entities: Organisation of Young Doctors in Tunisia
insights.so_what: Grid failure during extreme heat now has a measurable body count—a template for climate-driven political instability in Mediterranean states.
insights.locator: The demonstrations followed several protests in Tunisian cities

themes.theme: Tunisia five years into Saied's decree rule

insights.claim: Thousands demonstrated in Tunis on July 25, 2026 to mark five years since President Kais Saied suspended parliament, declared a national emergency, and began ruling by decree, ostensibly to fight other politicians' 'hypocrisy, treachery, and robbery.'
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: The anniversary has become a fixed annual mobilization date—a predictable political-risk calendar item for Tunisian sovereign exposure.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, thousands of Tunisians demonstrated in the capital

insights.claim: Tunisia's economy grew just 2.5 percent last year versus an African average of 4.4 percent, with high youth unemployment, indicating that concentrated executive rule under Saied has coincided with material underperformance of the continental benchmark.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: A near-2-point growth gap to the African average quantifies the cost of Tunisia's authoritarian turn and pressures debt sustainability.
insights.locator: Both Libya and Tunisia have seen several anti-government protests

insights.claim: Analyst Ikram Ben Said argues in Nawaat that concentrated executive rule has not and structurally cannot fix Tunisia's basic services, framing the blackouts as evidence of a governance-design failure rather than a transient crisis.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: If service delivery cannot improve under the current structure, protest recurrence is structural—not a one-summer event to fade out.
insights.quote: The outage underway this summer demonstrates that concentrated executive rule has not, and structurally cannot, fix Tunisia’s basic services
insights.locator: Demonstrations have not led to major political change

insights.claim: Tunisian detention conditions have become a mobilizing grievance, with the Committee for the Respect of Freedoms and Human Rights warning on July 24 that cells had 'turned into ovens' and 85-year-old opposition leader Rached Ghannouchi collapsing in detention from the heat.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: A prominent detainee death would be an escalation trigger; watch prisoner-health reporting as a leading indicator of unrest intensity.
insights.locator: Rached Ghannouchi, an 85-year-old opposition leader

insights.claim: Anti-government demonstrations in both Libya and Tunisia have repeatedly failed to produce major political change, meaning protest frequency is a poor predictor of regime turnover in North Africa.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: Base rates argue against pricing regime change off protest headlines; the tradable effect is infrastructure disruption, not transition.
insights.locator: Demonstrations have not led to major political change

insights.claim: The Iran war's push on oil and basic commodity prices is expected to generate more protests across Africa, and some governments are preemptively cracking down—Tanzania banned a July 7 protest that never occurred and still arrested nearly 200 people including 51 opposition members.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: The oil shock's political transmission into Africa is preemptive repression, not just street unrest—raising sanction and governance risk for frontier exposures.
insights.locator: As war in Iran continues to push up prices of oil

themes.theme: U.S. pressure dismantling the ICC in francophone Africa

insights.claim: Chad withdrew from the International Criminal Court following a direct call from Frank Garcia, Trump's new assistant secretary of state for African affairs, in which the American side 'called on Chad to review its accession to the Rome Statute.'
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: Washington is actively brokering ICC exits, showing bilateral leverage over African states is being spent on institutional demolition rather than commercial or security aims.
insights.quote: The American side expressed its concerns about the functioning of this institution and called on Chad to review its accession to the Rome Statute
insights.locator: Chad leaves ICC

insights.claim: Chad follows Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger in exiting the ICC, and justified it by noting nine of the court's 13 cases since founding concerned African states, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio vowed earlier this month to dismantle the court 'brick by brick.'
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: A cascading exodus from an international legal institution—one of the clearest measurable indicators of multilateral order erosion.
insights.locator: Chad became the latest francophone African country

insights.claim: Chad has an independent motive for avoiding the ICC because U.N. experts found it may be facilitating arms transfers from the UAE to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, just as the ICC announced a breakthrough in investigating RSF attacks on El Geneina and El Fasher that the U.N. said had 'hallmarks of genocide.'
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: The ICC exit doubles as legal cover for an active UAE-Sudan arms pipeline—relevant to Gulf reputational risk and Sudan conflict duration.
insights.locator: There’s at least one additional geopolitical reason

themes.theme: Senegal, South Africa, and Sahel political flashpoints

insights.claim: Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye launched a new party, the Republican Patriots, splitting from Prime Minister-turned-rival Ousmane Sonko's Pastef, after clashing over IMF debt negotiations and dismissing Sonko in May—with Sonko then elected president of the National Assembly and refusing to join the June government.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: Pastef's parliamentary majority now sits with the president's rival, directly jeopardizing the IMF deal—material for Senegalese eurobond spreads.
insights.locator: Senegal’s new party

insights.claim: A South African court has temporarily frozen the 31-member parliamentary impeachment committee examining Cyril Ramaphosa over the undeclared theft of $580,000 stored in a sofa at his Phala Phala game farm, and even if the process resumes he is unlikely to be voted out.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: Low probability of South African leadership change from this channel—removes a tail risk that periodically resurfaces in ZAR pricing.
insights.locator: Unlikely impeachment

insights.claim: The Trump administration is reportedly weighing military action against Islamist militants in Mali similar to recent airstrikes in Nigeria, but Mali—which partners with Russia's Africa Corps—says it received no confirmation and insists any intervention must respect its 'sovereign choices.'
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: U.S. strikes inside a Russian-partnered state would be a new escalation vector in the Sahel; Nigeria has already set the precedent.
insights.locator: U.S. strikes in Mali?

themes.theme: Chinese capital surges into African megaprojects

insights.claim: Chinese Belt and Road investments in Africa nearly tripled year-over-year in the first half of 2026 to a historic $33.5 billion, according to the Green Finance and Development Center and the University of Queensland.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: A tripling in six months is the single largest capital-flow shift in the brief—Chinese EPC contractors, and African construction and power supply chains, are the direct beneficiaries.
insights.locator: Africa is once again China’s top destination for megaprojects

insights.claim: Chinese manufacturers are being drawn to Africa specifically by the continent's preferential trade access to U.S. and EU markets, making African production a tariff-arbitrage route rather than purely a resource play.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: Tariff walls against China are being routed around via African assembly—watch for U.S./EU rules-of-origin tightening as the countermeasure.
insights.locator: The authors suggest that Chinese manufacturers are attracted

insights.claim: Flagship Chinese projects include a nearly $15 billion renewable energy and ammonia project in Ethiopia, a $10 billion steel mill in Egypt, and $1.4 billion for grid expansion and the Tazara railway in Zambia—an explicit rival to the U.S.-backed Lobito Corridor.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: Tazara versus Lobito is the concrete infrastructure contest for Central African copper export routing—decisive for who controls critical-mineral logistics.
insights.locator: Big-ticket projects include a nearly $15 billion

insights.claim: UNCTAD's annual report shows Chinese companies were the largest investors in African greenfield projects last year, including a $2.5 billion crude oil refinery in Ethiopia, a $1.1 billion refinery in Zambia, and $1.1 billion to expand a copper mine in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
insights.speaker: Nosmot Gbadamosi
insights.so_what: China is building downstream refining and mine capacity in Africa simultaneously—vertical integration of the critical-minerals chain outside Western reach.
